title: State v. Laxmi Mishra
court: Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
result: Convicted u/s 135; posted for sentence (obstruction case; no settlement; wires removed by accused before seizure)
statutes: Third proviso to Section 135(1) Electricity Act 2003

interpretations.interpretation: Illegal tapping from the licensee's distribution box to unmetered premises is a clause (a) connection; where the occupant obstructs and removes the wires, the tap and load may still be proved by the officials' testimony, the videographed proceedings and the load taken on the accused's own disclosure. 'Dishonestly' takes its s.24 IPC meaning.

Compulsory presumption on proof of an unauthorised means (Neeraj Dutt); rebuttal on the prudent-man standard (Hiten P. Dalal). A bare, unproved plea (here, solar power) cannot rebut it; only proof of lawful metered use / paid bills discharges the s.106 onus (Mukesh Rastogi).

Inspection power and ID safeguards (60); contemporaneous report, seizure/sealing, photo/video documentation (61) — seizure could not be completed because the accused removed the wires, but the inspection remained valid; prosecution procedure (62); assessment at twice tariff (63). No procedural lapse suggested.

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: An inspection report prepared by officers in discharge of official duty carries a presumption of regularity; onus on the consumer to rebut by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity to the accused.

citations.case: Balu Sudam Khalde v. State of Maharashtra
citations.principle: Incriminating suggestions put by defence counsel in cross-examination bind the accused and can establish facts such as the factum of, and presence at, the inspection.
'Shall presume' denotes a compulsory legal presumption the court is bound to draw until the fact is disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: Rebuttal of a statutory presumption need not be conclusive; evidence must make the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is production of paid electricity bills; Section 106 Evidence Act places that onus on the consumer.

significance.point: Obstruction is a circumstance of guilt
significance.explanation: Refusing to open the premises, removing the tapped wires, and giving a false name were read as malafide conduct pointing to involvement, not gaps in the prosecution.

significance.point: The load can be proved without seizing the wires
significance.explanation: Where the accused spirits away the case property, the load taken physically on her own disclosure plus the videographed proceedings still prove the theft.
Giving inspectors a wrong name ('Geeta'), exposed in investigation, corroborated dishonest intention.

significance.point: An unproved solar-power plea is no rebuttal
significance.explanation: A bare suggestion of solar power, unsupported by evidence, cannot discharge the third-proviso onus — only paid bills / lawful metered use (s.106, Mukesh Rastogi).

significance.point: Defence questions can admit the inspection
significance.explanation: Asking the videographer about the handycam admitted the factum of videography (Balu Sudam Khalde).
Official inspection testimony, videographed and 65B-certified, suffices absent shown enmity (Ashwani Kumar; Sushil Sharma).
